List of first human settlements - Wiki

_: Recent finds of stone tools in Jwalapuram before and after the Toba supereruption , may have been made by modern humans, but this is disputed.
Bones found in a cave near Beijing in 1958 have been radiocarbon dated at between 39-42,000 years old.
Stone, bone, and wood artifacts and animal and plant remains found in Washington County, Pennsylvania.
Early humans travelled by sea and spread from mainland Asia eastward to New Guinea and Australia.
Charcoal from the oldest layers yielded dates of 41,000-56,000 BP.

The Omo remains found in 1967 near the Ethiopian Kibish Mountains, have been dated as ca. 195,000 years old, making them the earliest human remains ever found. They are older than the remains found at Herto Bouri , Ethiopia (155-160,000 BP).
Genetic research indicates arrival of humans in Japan by 37,000 BP. Archeological remains at the Tategahana Paleolithic Site at Lake Nojiri have been dated as early as 47,000 BP.
Skeleton of 8-10 year old child discovered in 1994.

Archaeologists, Dr. Armand Mijares with Dr. Phil Piper found bones in a cave near Peñablanca, Cagayan in 2010 have been dated as ca. 67,000 years old. It's the earliest human fossil ever found in Asia-Pacific.
Semliki harpoon heads carved from bone.

Three Paleolithic flutes belonging to the early Aurignacian , which is associated with the assumed earliest presence of Homo sapiens in Europe ( Cro-Magnon ). It is the oldest example of prehistoric music .
Human jaw fragment found in Torquay, Devon in 1927.
The cave paintings in the Chauvet Cave in southern France have been called the earliest known cave art, though the dating is uncertain.

Remains found in the Klasies River Caves in the Eastern Cape province of South Africa show signs of human hunting. There is some debate as to whether these remains represent anatomically modern humans.
Two baby teeth discovered in Apulia in 1964 are the earliest modern human remains yet found in Europe.
Stone, bone and charcoal artifacts.
Anatomically modern human discovered 1924 with rare temporal bone pathology.
Spear heads and human fossils.

Human-worked mammoth bone flakes found at Bluefish Caves, Yukon, are much older than the stone tools and animal remains at Haida Gwaii in British Columbia (10-12,000 BP) and indicate the earliest known human settlement in North America .
Anatomically modern human remains of uncertain date, 90-190,000 years old.
A boomerang made from mammoth tusk.

A human skull in Sarawak, Borneo, has been dated to ca. 34-46,000 years ago. (Archeologists have claimed a much earlier date for stone tools found in the Mansuli valley, near Lahad Datu in Sabah , but precise dating analysis has not yet been published.)
Stone and bone artifacts found in a cave of the Ayacucho complex.
The population of Madagascar seems to have derived in equal measures from Borneo and East Africa.

The oldest human skeletal remains are the 40,000-year-old Lake Mungo remains in New South Wales, but human ornaments discovered at Devil's Lair in Western Australia have been dated to 48,000 BP. Ochre fragments at Malakunanja II in Northern Territory are dated to ca. 45,000 BP.
The earliest remains of anatomically modern man, based on radiocarbon dating of charcoal, have been found in the Fa Hien Cave in western Sri Lanka.
Chipped stone tool similar to those of the Changpin culture on the east coast.
Carbon dating of remains from this site represent the oldest known settlement in South America .
Bones dated as 38–42,000 years old are among the oldest human remains found in Europe.
Laang Spean cave in the Stung Sangker River valley, Battambang Province.
Stone tools made by anatomically modern humans.
Oldest human bones that clearly represent a human settlement in Europe.
Possible Neanderthal/Cro-Magnon hybrid, the Lapedo child.

The first settlement dates back to the Palaeolithic era. Geneticist Bryan Sykes identifies 'Ursula' as the first of The Seven Daughters of Eve and the carrier of the mitochondrial haplogroup U . This hypothetical woman moved between the mountain caves and the coast of Greece, …
Discovered in 1929-1935; remains exhibit a mix of archaic and modern traits and may represent an early migration from Africa that died out by 80,000 years ago.

In 2009 an ancient skull was recovered from a cave in the Annamite Mountains in northern Laos which is at least 46,000 years old, making it the oldest modern human fossil found to date in Southeast Asia.
Fragments of two human mandibles discovered in 1953.

Tools found in the Dhofar Governorate correspond with African objects from the so-called 'Nubian Complex', dating from 75-125,000 years ago. According to archaeologist Jeffrey I. Rose, human settlements spread east from Africa across the Arabian Peninsula.
The oldest remnants of the so-called Fosna culture were found in Aukra in Møre og Romsdal , and date from this period.
Carbon dating of hazel nut shells reveals this place to have been inhabited for 9,700 years.

Though some researchers suggest settlements as early as 50–150 AD, that later went extinct, it is generally accepted that the islands were permanently settled by Eastern Polynesians (the ancestors of the Māori ) who arrived about 1250–1300 AD.
Carbon dating of burial site.
Burned bones of megafauna.
The Pulli settlement on the bank of the Pärnu River briefly pre-dates that at Kunda , which gave its name to the Kunda culture.
First settled by Dutch under Cornelius Gooyer.
Radiocarbon dating of a shell midden at Bourewa on Viti Levu Island shows earliest inhabitation at 1220-970 BC.
Settlers from Sicily brought agriculture and impressed ware pottery.
Settlers from Portugal.
Ingólfr Arnarson , the first known Norse settler, built his homestead in Reykjavík this year, though Norse or Hiberno-Scottish monks might have arrived up to two hundred years earlier.
Lapita pottery found at Teouma cemetery on Efate and on several other islands.
Lapita site found at Mulifanua Ferry Berth Site by New Zealand scientists in the 1970s.
Radiocarbon dating of a shell found at the site dates the occupation at 3180±100 BP.
Settled by English survivors of the Sea Venture shipwreck, led by George Somers.
Agricultural remains from three locations were analysed and dated to as early as the sixth century A.D.
Saqqaq culture was the first of several waves of settlement from northern Canada and from Scandinavia.
Evidence of fire in a submerged cave last accessible 8000 BP.
Settled by French during the expedition of Louis Antoine de Bougainville.
